input:
This memo recommends a three-month pilot of bearing condition sensors on 20 pumps, at a cost of $31k, before any decision about a full installation across the whole fleet. The pilot would be run by the reliability engineering group, and the decision on full installation held until the pilot results are reported, in time for the March capital review, when the decision can be taken on evidence gathered at this plant rather than figures supplied by others.

There are 214 pumps running at the plant, and the maintenance records covering the last 12 months show 1119 h of unplanned downtime. Bearing failures account for 40% of the downtime hours, which works out, as a derived figure, at 447.6 h attributable to bearing failures over the period. This concentration of downtime in a single failure mode makes bearing monitoring an attractive candidate, since a sensor package aimed at bearings is directed at the largest single identified contributor to lost running time.

A sensor set covering all 214 pumps is quoted at $386k installed, plus a further $65k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 28%, although this figure is a vendor figure, generated elsewhere, and was not measured at this plant. It indicates the possible scale of the prize, but it does not by itself demonstrate what would actually be achieved here. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: the sensors improve detection but do not shorten supply, so any benefit still depends on parts being available when a deteriorating bearing is identified.

The pilot is a measured next step. For $31k, three months on 20 pumps will show how the sensors perform on this plant's pumps, records and crews, and the reliability engineering group will report before the March capital review. The decision on full installation is held until that evidence is available, rather than prejudged in either direction.
target:
Recommendation: run a three-month pilot of bearing sensors on 20 pumps at $31k, owned by the reliability engineering group, and hold the decision on full installation until the pilot results are reported to the March capital review.

The plant runs 214 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1119 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 40% of the downtime hours, a derived 447.6 h. Unplanned downtime is running time lost outside a planned outage. The bearing share makes bearings the largest single named cause in the record, and a sensor set aimed at bearings addresses that share rather than downtime in general. The record is a count of hours, not of events, so a cause that stops a pump for long periods weighs more heavily in it than a cause that stops pumps often but briefly.

Full installation is quoted at $386k installed for all 214 pumps, plus $65k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 28%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so it sizes the prize without evidencing the saving here. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: detection improves, supply does not, and downtime avoided still depends on parts being on hand when a bearing is flagged.

The pilot bounds the commitment. Three months on 20 pumps tests detection on this plant's pumps, records and crews at $31k, against a full-installation decision that is held, not pre-judged, until the reliability engineering group reports. The March capital review then decides with plant data in place of the vendor figure, and the quoted full-fleet cost stands unchanged as the figure that decision will weigh. The pilot also fixes what the vendor trial cannot: whether the warning the sensors give arrives early enough, on this plant's bearings, for a repair to be planned rather than improvised.
